1. The animation compares the total interest paid on a mortgage under three plans. A 30-year loan on its normal schedule costs $477,622 in interest. The same 30-year loan paid off in 15 years by making extra payments costs $210,691. A true 15-year loan costs $189,069. The stacks of green cash show these amounts. Later frames show a character, Tessa, standing by a house. A gold stack, labeled "the stack," moves next to the house, and two white columns stand nearby.

2. In frames 1 and 2 the camera zooms in on the cash stacks. The gold slice in frame 2 appears to mark the gap between the two 15-year outcomes ($210,691 versus $189,069). In frame 3 the gold stack lifts off and lands beside Tessa's house. In frames 4 and 5 the gold stack sits next to the house while the white columns stay to the side. In frame 6 two dark, faded columns appear on the left and some small gray blocks float above the house. I can't tell from the image alone what those represent.

3. The most direct reading is that paying off a loan early saves a lot of interest, and that a 30-year loan prepaid over 15 years still costs somewhat more than a real 15-year loan. That is because the 15-year loan has a lower rate. The later frames seem to use Tessa as an example of one person's choice about where a "stack" of money goes: toward the house, or somewhere else, shown by the white columns. The labels "ILLUSTRATIVE," "US only," and "history, not a forecast" mark this as a hypothetical, not a prediction. The citation to the Freddie Mac weekly mortgage survey suggests the rates come from that source.

4. The image doesn't state any advice. A viewer could take away that paying down a mortgage early saves a lot of interest. They might also take away that the choice between prepaying and investing is a trade-off, since the animation sets the house stack against the separate columns. The animation gives no verdict on which is better, and the "history, not a forecast" label warns against reading it as a prediction.

5. The animation suggested the interest figures and the idea of comparing loan paths, because those appear in the labels. Any advice in 4 is my own conclusion. The picture and text give no recommendation, and I can't say what the white and dark columns stand for.
